articles.title: Kenya’s Ebola cases test preparedness beyond Nairobi
articles.summary: The scare exposed gaps in how far outbreak readiness reaches Kenya’s remote communities.
articles.body:
Nairobi, Kenya – Kenya’s response to an imported Ebola case has demonstrated its ability to mobilise a national response in the capital.

But a suspected case in the northeastern county of Wajir has raised a critical question: whether the country’s preparedness measures can protect communities far from major hospitals, laboratories and transport hubs.

The suspected case in Wajir tested negative, according to county officials, easing fears of wider transmission. Yet the incident highlighted the importance of local health facilities being able to recognise suspected infections, isolate patients safely and communicate reliable information to residents.

For communities near Kenya’s borders, preparedness requires more than screening travellers at airports and official crossings.

It also depends on trained health workers, appropriate protective equipment, functioning isolation facilities and clear referral procedures. Residents must know where to seek care and how to respond when health authorities raise the alarm.

Garad Saney Mohamed, communications director for Wajir county, told Al Jazeera that the county had established an isolation centre in Wajir town and formed a rapid response team to strengthen its preparedness.

He said the county was also using radio campaigns, community health promoters, school health programmes and posters to raise awareness about Ebola. A preparedness plan and budget had been put in place, he added.

However, the county did not provide details on the isolation centre’s capacity, the number of health workers trained specifically in Ebola response or the budget allocated to these efforts. Without that information, it is difficult to assess whether the county has the personnel and resources needed to manage suspected infections safely or respond to a wider outbreak.

The suspected case involved a 20-year-old man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo through Uganda before reaching his home in Wajir on September 20. He was assessed at Habaswein Subcounty Hospital in Wajir South after presenting with a severe febrile illness.

His sample tested negative for Ebola, according to county officials. He was to remain under observation while receiving medical care.

The case prompted precautionary action, but it does not establish whether Wajir’s wider preparedness systems would be sufficient during an outbreak. That would depend on factors including the availability of protective equipment, staff trained in infection prevention and control, safe sample transport and reliable links between local facilities and designated testing laboratories.

Wajir’s proximity to Somalia, which lies 110km (70 miles) to the east, and the movement of people and goods across the border make surveillance and public communication particularly important. Screening at formal entry points remains essential, but it cannot replace the ability of local health facilities and community health workers to recognise warning signs and guide people towards appropriate care.

Kenya’s national response intensified after an Ebola case was linked to a Kenyan travelling from the Democratic Republic of the Congo through Uganda. The patient arrived in Nairobi on October 3, was diagnosed with Bundibugyo virus of the disease and died on October 5, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Kenya notified the WHO on October 6.

The patient had fallen ill while living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and travelled by road to Kampala before flying to Nairobi. Laboratory tests at the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute confirmed the infection, according to the Ministry of Health.

On October 14, Kenya confirmed a second case of Bundibugyo virus disease involving a 39-year-old man who was a close family member of the first patient. He was already in quarantine and under daily monitoring when he developed symptoms, including fever, fatigue and joint pains, on October 13.

Laboratory tests confirmed the infection, and he was transferred to a designated treatment centre for supportive care. The Ministry of Health said the two cases were linked and there was no evidence of transmission in the wider community.

Authorities subsequently intensified surveillance at points of entry, contact tracing and public communication. The negative test result in Wajir underscored the importance of investigating suspected infections promptly and using laboratory testing to establish whether the virus is present.

As of October 6, Kenya had screened 652,584 travellers, tested 267 samples and trained 4,971 healthcare workers in Ebola prevention and management, according to the Ministry of Health.

By October 12, the WHO reported that more than 665,000 travellers had been screened and 127 contacts had been listed, with 94 in quarantine. Five laboratories had been designated to test for the disease, and nearly 5,000 health workers had received training.

These figures demonstrate the scale of the national response. But the number of travellers screened or health workers trained does not, on its own, establish how effectively those resources are distributed or whether individual counties can manage suspected infections.

For Wajir, the key questions concern the readiness of local facilities, the availability of trained personnel and protective equipment, and the speed with which samples can be transported for testing. The county has outlined the measures it has taken, but the available information does not provide a complete picture of its operational capacity.

Preparedness means more than the numbers

Health workers need to recognise suspected cases, follow infection-prevention protocols, collect and transport samples safely, and refer patients without exposing others. Facilities must also have appropriate protective equipment and clear procedures for managing suspected infections.

The WHO reported that Kenya’s national preparedness score rose from 66 percent in May to 82 percent in July. The assessment covered measures including surveillance, laboratory testing, isolation and treatment facilities, and trained response teams.

The improvement suggests that preparedness measures had advanced before the imported case was confirmed. However, a national score cannot establish whether every county has the equipment, staffing and referral arrangements needed to respond effectively. Assessments of local capacity are essential to identifying gaps that national figures may not reveal.

The Kenya Red Cross has also supported preparedness and public awareness efforts. Dr Paul Olale, a representative of the organisation, told Al Jazeera about a preparedness assessment. However, the basis of the separate figure attributed to the organisation was not established in the information available for this report, making it difficult to determine what it measured or whether it identified county-level weaknesses.

The organisation has highlighted the need to counter misinformation. During an outbreak, rumours can leave people uncertain about symptoms, how the virus spreads and whether they should seek medical attention.

For residents, information needs to be practical. People should know where to seek care, how to report a suspected illness and what to do while awaiting medical advice. Communication must also address stigma and reassure people that reporting a suspected illness can help protect their families and communities.

Community health promoters, local radio stations, schools and trusted community leaders can help deliver information in languages and formats residents understand. But awareness campaigns are most effective when they are consistent and backed by health services capable of responding promptly to concerns.

Wajir’s experience illustrates why Kenya’s Ebola preparedness must be measured not only by national screening figures and training totals, but also by the ability of individual counties to respond safely when a suspected case emerges.

An isolation centre, a rapid response team and public awareness campaigns are important components of an effective response. Their existence alone, however, does not establish whether facilities have adequate equipment, staff can follow established protocols or residents can access reliable information when they need it.

Kenya has demonstrated its ability to mobilise a national response, expand screening and undertake laboratory testing. The challenge is ensuring that these measures translate into effective protection beyond major transport hubs, including in remote communities where access to healthcare and timely information may be more difficult.

Dr Mary Muthoni, Kenya’s principal secretary for public health and professional standards, underscored the importance of protecting frontline staff in remarks delivered on behalf of Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, according to a WHO statement released on October 12.

“No health worker in this country should be asked to attend to a suspected Ebola case without the right protective equipment.”

articles.title: Can drinking coriander water help in melting belly fat?
articles.summary: Whether you are trying to fix your health or simply want to lose weight, just starting with one fad drink in the morning may not work like a miracle!
articles.body: Whether you are trying to fix your health or simply want to lose weight, just starting with one fad drink in the morning may not work like a miracle! And that’s the same thing with coriander water, which has many benefits for health but cannot totally melt away the stubborn belly fat. In fact, it is one of the biggest myths that one morning drink can fix and melt visceral body fat in just one or two days. However, being consistent with diet and workouts and then adding coriander water (dhaniya water) may effectively help in reducing waistline. Coriander water has gained massive popularity as a miracle belly fat burner; this is because of the compounds in coriander. Here’s all you need to know about it…What study saysNo beverage or food can target or melt fat from a specific area of the body, such as the belly. According to research published in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, localized fat reduction is a biological impossibility. When the body enters a caloric deficit, it mobilizes stored triglycerides from fat cells across the entire body, governed by genetics, hormones, and overall energy balance, not by localized digestive activity.What coriander water actually does for the digestive systemCoriander seeds (Coriandrum sativum) contain bioactive compounds, including linalool and borneol, which act as natural carminatives. A study published in Digestive Diseases and Sciences noted that coriander extract helps relax tract muscles, aiding in gas relief and improving overall bowel motility. By easing indigestion and trapped gas coriander water can visibly flatten a distended stomach giving the appearance of a waistline without actual loss of fat mass.Fluid retention and the diuretic effectMany individuals report initial weight changes after drinking coriander water daily, but this is primarily water weight rather than fat mass. As per another research evaluating extracts in Phytotherapy Research coriander acts as a mild natural diuretic, encouraging the kidneys to excrete excess sodium and fluid. Flushing out excess fluid reduces puffiness and abdominal fluid retention, leading to drops on the bathroom scale.Impact on blood sugar and metabolismControlling glucose spikes plays a role in long-term body composition management. In animal models published in the British Journal of Nutrition, coriander seed supplementation was shown to stimulate insulin secretion and enhance glucose uptake into cells stabilizing blood sugar levels. While stable glucose levels help regulate appetite and reduce energy crashes, human clinical trials have not demonstrated that coriander intake alone significantly boosts resting metabolic rate or drives oxidation.The bottom lineCoriander water is a low-calorie, hydrating beverage that can support healthy digestion, reduce bloating, and help with maintaining fluid balance. However, the current scientific literature confirms that it does not possess burning properties capable of melting belly fat. Sustained reduction of fat requires a consistent energy deficit achieved through balanced nutrition, movement, and lifestyle habits.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Jalna juvenile gets six-month community service for kidnapping 13-year-old, demanding Rs 5 cr ransom
articles.summary: Jalna Juvenile Justice Board orders six months’ community service for juvenile convicted of kidnapping a 13-year-old and demanding Rs 5 crore ransom; boy rescued safe.
articles.body: Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar: A juvenile found guilty of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy and demanding a ransom of Rs 5 crore has been directed by Juvenile Justice Board, Jalna, to perform community service at the children’s ward of the district general hospital for six months.In an order passed on Monday, the board directed the juvenile to render community service every Monday and Wednesday. The juvenile was held guilty under IPC sections related to kidnapping, kidnapping for ransom, voluntarily causing hurt, criminal intimidation, common intention and criminal conspiracy.The order followed a trial in which the prosecution examined 17 witnesses, including the complainant, the victim, panch witnesses, then additional superintendent of police Ayush Nopani and investigating officer B B Narode. Assistant public prosecutor Atik E Parkote represented the prosecution.According to the prosecution, the incident occurred on June 25, 2024, when the child left home for school at 8am in the morning but never reached class. The father had left for his shop after the boy left for school. Later that day, at 11.45am, the father received a call from unidentified persons claiming to have the boy in their custody and demanding Rs 5 crore for his release. The callers allegedly threatened to kill the child if the ransom was not paid.After being alerted, then additional superintendent of police Ayush Nopani formed two teams to trace the child and apprehend the accused. Police laid a trap and arrested two accused when they arrived to collect the ransom money. The boy was rescued safely from a van and reunited with his family.The prosecution alleged that the child was confined for several hours at an undisclosed location. During the ordeal, he was allegedly slapped and punched, his mouth restrained with a handkerchief, and he was threatened with death if the ransom demand was not met.Following the investigation, sub-inspector B B Narode filed the final report before Juvenile Justice Board. The board, headed by principal magistrate S N Pund and members A M Dhannawat and R B Jagtap, considered the evidence and arguments before delivering the order.Stay updated with the latest Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar news. articles.title: Gangster Dilawar’s aide on ventilator after health deteriorates in Harsul jail
articles.summary: Syed Nazer Ali, aide of jailed gangster Shaikh Imran “Dilawar” Mehandi, fell ill in Harsul Central Prison and was shifted to GMCH Aurangabad, now on ventilator.
articles.body: Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar: Syed Nazer Ali, a close associate of jailed gangster Shaikh Imran Mehandi, alias Dilawar, and a co-accused in several high-profile murder cases, is battling for life after his health suddenly deteriorated inside Harsul Central Prison. He was shifted to Govt Medical College and Hospital on Sunday evening and remains on ventilator support.Doctors said following preliminary examinations, Nazer Ali underwent dialysis before being placed on a ventilator. “He continues to remain under medical supervision,” a senior GMCH doctor said.Confirming the development, Harsul Central Prison in-charge superintendent Anil Khamkar said, “Nazer Ali, a life convict lodged in barrack 8 of the old circle, complained of dizziness and started vomiting. He was shifted to GMCH immediately and is now on ventilator support.”Nazer Ali is considered one of the key members of Dilawar’s gang and is a co-accused in multiple murder cases registered in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar in 2012. The cases include the murders of former corporator Salim Qureshi, Nilesh Mhatre, Shaikh Naser, Sindubai Mhatre and Sirajuddin.The development comes days after Supreme Court granted relief to Dilawar in the 2012 Salim Qureshi murder case by suspending his life sentence pending disposal of his appeal. The apex court took into account his prolonged incarceration, including 12 years without remission and 18 years with remission.Despite the relief, Dilawar remains behind bars as he stands convicted in another murder case and continues to face trial in three others. Nazer Ali and several other associates are also accused in those cases.The circumstances behind Nazer Ali’s sudden medical emergency were not immediately known.Stay updated with the latest Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar news. articles.title: San Jose girl, 8, dies after living in cockroach-infested home as mother, stepfather face charges
articles.summary: Aurora Williams lived in a cockroach-infested San Jose home with mold and pet feces before a fatal asthma attack, which prompted felony charges against her mother and stepfather.
articles.body: An 8-year-old California girl died following a severe asthma attack after allegedly living for years in a filthy home infested with cockroaches, mold and pet feces, prompting felony child neglect charges against her mother and stepfather, prosecutors said. The Santa Clara County District Attorney's Office said this week that the girl's mother, Gabrielle Hanson, 32, and stepfather, Jacob Randolph, 39, knew about the dangerous conditions inside their San Jose home and had been repeatedly warned by medical professionals and social workers about the risks to their seven children. Despite the warnings, the couple allegedly waited eight hours before seeking medical help when their daughter, Aurora Williams, began experiencing serious medical distress in May. "It was too late," prosecutors said in a news release announcing the charges. SOUTH CAROLINA MOM COULDN'T REMEMBER LAST TIME SHE FED 2 DAUGHTERS BEFORE THEY WERE FOUND DEAD: AFFIDAVITS In February 2025, more than a year before her death, Aurora was taken to an emergency room by a relative after experiencing asthma symptoms, wheezing and difficulty breathing, according to prosecutors. A bug fell from her shoe and a cockroach was seen crawling on her, prompting her to tell staff, "Oh yeah, bugs just crawl on me." Hospital staff also reported that Aurora smelled like cat urine, appeared seriously underweight and pale, and said she was hungry and had not eaten. On May 13, 2026, San Jose police and firefighters responded to the family's home for a medical emergency involving a child. CALIFORNIA COUPLE CHARGED WITH ABUSING 14 SURROGATE-BORN CHILDREN INSIDE $10M LOS ANGELES MANSION Six other children, ranging in age from 2 months to 17 years, were taken into protective custody by social workers. Aurora was declared dead four days later, according to prosecutors. The medical examiner determined that Aurora died from a lack of oxygen to the brain caused by severe asthma and an acute lung injury associated with a viral infection. Medical neglect was identified as a significant contributing factor, and her death was ruled a homicide. Investigators determined that Aurora and her siblings had been living in "squalid and dangerous conditions" since at least 2019, according to prosecutors. Detectives also found that Aurora's asthma equipment had not been properly maintained and that her prescribed inhaler was missing during two searches of the home. COLORADO MOM ALLEGEDLY BOUGHT ALCOHOL DAILY FOR 16-YEAR-OLD DAUGHTER FOUND DEAD WITH 173 EMPTY BOTTLES Investigators later discovered a dirty inhaler spacer missing a rubber seal designed to prevent medication from leaking, along with a respiratory mask containing cockroaches. "Another child is needlessly dead in this county, and once again our prosecutors will do everything in our legal power to hold the people who did this responsible," District Attorney Jeff Rosen said in a statement. "Prosecuting people after this kind of tragedy is necessary — and not enough," Rosen continued. "There are serious questions about how this child and her siblings lived in this dangerous squalor for so long. In the name of this lost child and the others, this community deserves honest answers and real changes." The investigation also led to child sexual abuse charges against Aurora's maternal uncle, Jonathan Hanson, 44, involving another child in the home. CALIFORNIA PASTOR CHARGED WITH YEARSLONG CHILD MOLESTATION AS INVESTIGATORS SEEK MORE VICTIMS: DA Prosecutors charged Jonathan Hanson with two counts of molestation and one count of possessing explicit videos of the alleged victim, who was between 11 and 15 years old at the time of the alleged offenses. Gabrielle Hanson, the alleged victim's stepmother, was also charged with knowing about the alleged abuse and failing to intervene, prosecutors said. All three defendants were arraigned Tuesday. Gabrielle Hanson and Randolph were released under supervised own recognizance over prosecutors' objections, while Jonathan Hanson was ordered held without bail. articles.title: Man claims he went blind after taking Ozempic, shares warning for other users
articles.summary: Todd Engel claims Ozempic caused his total vision loss from NAION and has filed a lawsuit against Novo Nordisk over inadequate drug warnings.
articles.body: A Maryland man claims that a popular weight-loss drug caused his total vision loss, leaving him legally blind. Todd Engel, 63, was first prescribed Ozempic in 2023 to help manage his diabetes. The GLP-1 medication, which is approved to treat type 2 diabetes, is also commonly prescribed off-label for weight loss. Approximately four months after starting the medication, Engel was diagnosed with nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS FACE NUMEROUS LAWSUITS OVER RARE ‘EYE STROKE’ LINKED TO VISION LOSS The condition, in which reduced blood flow damages the optic nerve, can cause sudden and permanent vision loss. "I first noticed it on New Year's Eve, 2024. I had just gotten out of the shower, was getting ready to go to work. And I said to Shelley, ‘I can't see in my right eye. It's totally black. It's totally dark in my right eye,’" Engel told Fox News Digital during an on-camera interview. "I was horrified. I was very, very upset that I couldn't see." DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS Engel was referred for further testing, including at Johns Hopkins’ Wilmer Eye Institute. He was told he had suffered an "eye stroke," another term used for NAION. "The blood work came back in the normal range for me. My blood pressure was fine. They said, ‘You can go back to work,’" he said. "I didn't go blind — I had my vision taken from me, which was catastrophic to me and to my family." Engel continued taking Ozempic because, according to the family's account, neither he nor his doctors knew of a possible association between semaglutide and NAION. About 10 months later, vision loss suddenly occurred in his left eye. "At that point in time, losing sight in both eyes, there was a tremendous amount of concern," he said. RAPID WEIGHT LOSS ON POPULAR DRUGS COULD ‘STARVE’ THE BRAIN, EXPERT WARNS Doctors told Engel there was no medication or surgical procedure that could restore his vision. Shelley Engel said that medical testing did not identify another common factor beyond Ozempic. Her husband immediately stopped taking the drug after losing vision in his second eye. "I didn't go blind — I had my vision taken from me, which was catastrophic to me and to my family," he said. Engel has filed a lawsuit against Novo Nordisk, the Denmark-based manufacturer of Ozempic, alleging that the company failed to adequately warn patients and doctors about the potential risk of vision loss. WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO 'OZEMPIC EARS' AND OTHER COSMETIC COMPLAINTS, SURGEONS SAY He is among hundreds of patients currently pursuing legal action against makers of GLP-1 medications, including Ozempic and Wegovy, over claims that the drugs caused NAION. The lawsuits allege that manufacturers failed to provide sufficient warnings about the potential risks, although a causal relationship between the medications and the condition has not been definitively established. Life after vision loss At the time of his vision loss, Engel was working for Howard County Highways as a heavy equipment operator and truck driver. He had worked in the field for about 40 years and held a commercial driver's license for nearly as long. "I was extremely mechanically inclined with my hands and in my mind. I can't do that anymore, which is extremely upsetting to me," he said. "People want to be able to retire on their own accord when they want to, not when a medical catastrophic injury such as this ... takes away your livelihood." PEOPLE ON WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS REPORT FINGERNAILS FALLING OFF AS RESEARCHERS UNCOVER SURPRISING LINK Beyond losing his career, Engel said even ordinary activities he once took for granted have become difficult. An avid reader before his vision loss, Engel said he can no longer read newspapers, magazines or books. Inside his home, he has learned to count steps to help navigate familiar spaces. 7 EVERYDAY MISTAKES COULD BE QUIETLY DAMAGING YOUR VISION, EYE DOCTOR WARNS "I know that coming in from our parking lot, there are 10 steps ... nine going down into our basement, 13 going up into our bedroom." Engel said he now uses a white cane to navigate outside his home and relies on his family for help with everyday activities. His four grandchildren often guide him during family gatherings. "They will take me by my hand and talk to me: ‘Pops, three steps straight. Then we're gonna turn right,’" he said. "For me personally, it's embarrassing. I'm 64 years old. I shouldn't need ... my grandchildren or my wife to help me get from point A to point B." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES His wife, Shelley Engel, said her husband's vision loss has affected the entire family. "It has completely changed every aspect of our lives," she said. "There is not one piece of our lives that hasn't changed or been touched by this throughout our whole family." For Engel, some of the most painful losses involve the things he can no longer do with the people closest to him. "I will never be able to see my wife's beautiful face again, be able to see children and grandchildren, be able to play ball with them," he said. "And that is very, very upsetting to me." "I wake up in the dark, I go to sleep in the darkness." A warning to others Engel said that if he had been warned about a possible link between Ozempic and vision loss, he would not have taken the drug. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Had I known, had my doctor had any inkling that this could have happened ... I'm sure he would have asked me and I would have said absolutely not," he said. "I will deal with the diabetes ... I refuse to jeopardize my eyes." The Engels said they are speaking publicly in hopes of preventing others from experiencing the same outcome. "Do the research for yourselves to make sure that my catastrophic injuries do not happen to you or anybody else," Engel said. "If we can help one person, then that's a pleasure to Shelley and I." ‘It's about information’ The family's attorney, Jonathan Orent, said the legal team is seeking a warning on the U.S. Ozempic label similar to information provided to patients and doctors in Europe. "It's amazing what just a simple warning can do," he told Fox News Digital. "That's really what this case is about. It's about information." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Company response Novo Nordisk, the Denmark-based company that makes Ozempic, has disputed that the medication causes NAION, stating that the available evidence does not establish a causal relationship between semaglutide and the eye condition. "Novo believes the personal injury lawsuits filed in the U.S. are without merit and we are defending them in court." "A causal relationship between GLP-1RAs, including semaglutide, and NAION cannot be confirmed based on the totality of data," Liz Skrbkova, head of U.S. Media and Stakeholder Relations for Novo Nordisk, told Fox News Digital. The company pointed to an analysis of its randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trials that found very few confirmed cases of NAION and no increased incidence among patients taking semaglutide. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Novo said it continues to monitor NAION as part of its routine drug-safety surveillance. "Novo believes the personal injury lawsuits filed in the U.S. are without merit, and we are defending them in court," Skrbkova said.

articles.title: NI health: Hospital doctors to strike as pay dispute continues
articles.summary: The British Medical Association says hospital doctors in Northern Ireland plan to strike in November.
articles.body:
Hospital doctors in Northern Ireland are to strike in November over pay.

It comes after the Royal College of Nursing announced that it is also balloting its members on potential strike action.

The doctors will stage two separate 24-hour strikes on 20 and 23 November.

The British Medical Association (BMA) has warned doctors are prepared to escalate the strike action if progress is not made in addressing the pay issue, which they say has seen doctors' pay drop from upwards of 26% over the past 18 years due to below inflation pay awards.

The Department of Health (DoH) has been approached for comment.

Resident doctors will hold a full 24-hour strike starting at 07:00 BST on 20 November until 07:00 the following morning.

Consultants and specialist, associate specialist and speciality grade (SAS) doctors will also take 24-hour action from 07:00 on 23 November until 07:00 the following morning.

They will provide what is known as Christmas Day cover, which means that most routine and elective services will be cancelled but full emergency cover will remain in place.

Resident doctors are fully qualified medical practitioners who are completing postgraduate clinical training in a hospital or general practice under the supervision of a senior doctor.

SAS doctors are specialist doctors employed by health trusts.

The three branches of hospital doctors also took strike action in June.

The BMA said if Health Minister Robbie Butler was serious about transforming the health service and addressing the waiting list crisis he needed to value doctors by paying them fairly.

Dr Clodagh Corrigan, chair of BMA's Northern Ireland SAS committee, said: "We have been clear to avoid further industrial action we need a credible offer from government that makes meaningful progress towards full pay restoration.

"We met with the new health minister recently, hopeful that we could begin fresh discussions on agreeing a credible pay offer. Regrettably, this did not happen."

She said the minister was unable to confirm if the minimum annual pay uplift for 2026/27, which has been paid to doctors elsewhere in the UK, would be paid "this side of Christmas, or indeed at all".

"We were informed that the decision ultimately lay with the executive," she said.

"Therefore, we have been left with no alternative but to announce more dates for industrial action and we are fully prepared to escalate action if no progress is made."

Dr David Farren, chair of BMA's NI consultants committee, said pay was central to recruitment and retention of doctors and hindered the delivery of a sustainable and safe health service.

"There is palpable anger among our members at continuing sub-inflationary, late pay awards while we work beyond capacity in under-supported services," he said.

"This annual uncertainty over when we will receive our pay award reinforces the widespread feeling that we are not valued, and leads to doctors seeking better paid roles elsewhere."

He said this impacted service delivery and it was "unacceptable that our government continues to let this happen".

It comes after the Royal College of Nursing announced on Wednesday that it will ballot its members on industrial action and strike action over pay.

The union said the move came after many months of inaction on the pay award.

Earlier this year, the NHS pay review body recommended a 3.3% pay increase for staff across all pay bands.

While nurses and healthcare workers in England and Wales have received their award, nursing staff in Northern Ireland have not.

In a statement the DoH said the health minister was clear that the 2026/27 award should be implemented and pay parity with colleagues in NHS England restored as soon as possible.

articles.title: East Singhbhum administration issues traffic plan for Durga Puja
articles.summary: East Singhbhum administration issues Jamshedpur traffic route plan for Durga Puja, with diversions and one-way rules in effect from Thursday till Oct 21.
articles.body: Jamshedpur: The East Singhbhum district administration on Thursday issued a traffic route map for the city to ensure smooth traffic movement during Durga Puja. articles.title: Want to Lower Blood Pressure? A Cardiologist Recommends This 1 Vegetable
articles.summary: How to lower blood pressure naturally with food. Cardiologist explains why beets are the best vegetable to manage hypertension and prevent stiff arteries.
articles.body: High blood pressure is a major risk factor for heart disease, so it’s important to keep it in check. It’s possible to lower blood pressure without medication by losing weight, exercising and eating a healthier diet. One vegetable in particular stands out, says Dr. Annapoorna Kini, a cardiologist at the Mount Sinai Fuster Heart Hospital in New York. Heart Health Tip of the Day: Add Beets to Your Diet “If you really want to know what decreases blood pressure, it is beet — beet root,” Kini tells TODAY.com. Beets contain nitrates, which get converted to nitric oxide in the body, and “plays an essential role in cardiovascular health,” researchers note. It’s a natural vasodilator, meaning it opens blood vessels, allowing greater blood flow. “It works on the (blood) vessel wall — dilates the smooth muscle of the vessel wall. That way, your vessel remains pliable,” Kini adds. Why It Matters Blood vessels become more rigid as people get older and start building up plaque in their arteries, Kini notes; and when the arteries get stiff, that’s how you develop high blood pressure. Arterial stiffness is a “leading marker of risk in hypertension,” researchers wrote in the journal Circulation Research. It also impacts the function of the brain and kidneys. Nitric oxide is a “potent vasodilator that opens the blood vessels and promotes blood flow throughout the body. This increase in blood flow results in less pressure in the arteries,” explained registered dietitian Natalie Rizzo, nutrition editor for TODAY, when writing about beet benefits. Beets are particularly high in nitrates, which the body turns into nitric oxide, and their juice has been shown to lower blood pressure. It’s one reason why beets make the list of cardiologists’ favorite vegetables. How to Get Started Juicing beets is a simple way to get a high amount of nitrates in one serving, Rizzo says. Try beet carrot ginger juice or Craig Melvin’s beet juice. Incorporate beets into your meals with a roasted beet salad with salmon or beet risotto. Beet greens, the vegetable’s leafy tops, are rich in nitrates. They’re also edible and delicious, Rizzo notes. She suggests sautéing them with some olive oil, garlic and salt for a healthy side dish, or adding them soups, smoothies and casseroles. Download the Start TODAY app for heart-healthy recipes, meal plans and workouts designed for every fitness level. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: Trans people should use hospital spaces according to biological sex, NHS England says
articles.summary: New guidance says trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex.
articles.body:
Trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex rather than their gender identity, according to new NHS England (NHSE) guidance.

It says when this is not "clinically appropriate" then alternative arrangements should be made and the dignity and safety of all patients should be maintained.

The guidance also says staff facilities should be used by people based on their biological sex, while trusts should ensure enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, such as single-occupancy toilets, are offered.

Previous NHSE guidance suggested patients and staff could be accommodated on wards or use facilities based on their gender identity.

That meant that a trans woman – a biological male who identifies as a woman – could have chosen to be on a women's ward, or a trans man – a biological female who identifies as a man – could have opted for a men's ward.

That guidance was withdrawn following the Supreme Court ruling in April 2025 that under equality law the term "sex" means biological sex and "woman" refers to a biological woman.

The judgment said for a space or service to be single sex it should only allow those of the same biological sex to use it.

Also under the new guidance issued on Thursday, NHSE emphasised that in order to avoid discriminating against trans people they should be offered gender neutral spaces.

But the guidance also says decisions may have to be made on a case-by-case basis and must ensure clinical needs are met.

It also makes clear that there are circumstances where clinical need is the overriding priority, including on emergency units and urgent care settings.

In addition to the patient document of the guidance, NHSE has published advice for trusts on how to organise changing rooms, toilets and other single-sex facilities for staff.

Again, it says they should be used by people based on their biological sex, not their gender identity.

The document encourages NHS trusts in England to carry out an audit to ensure they are offering enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, for instance, gender neutral or single occupancy toilets.

Pressures on hospitals mean many have already struggled to keep wards single sex.

NHSE data shows that the number of breaches of the previous mixed-sex accommodation guidance has been growing every year since 2021- where members of the opposite sex were placed on a single-sex ward.

The most recent figure for August 2026 shows there were 5,520 breaches, compared to 3,853 in June 2025.

Sex-based rights charity Sex Matters has welcomed the guidance as a "momentus shift back to reality", but is concerned about how it will be applied.

"NHS patient data is a mess, with potentially thousands of trans-identifying people recorded as the opposite sex," CEO Maya Forstater said.

Trans rights organisations TransActual and Trans+ Solidarity Alliance have said they are concerned NHS staff will be unclear on how to safely look after trans patients.

"This guidance will not survive contact with reality in resource-strapped hospitals and will create unworkable operational challenges," they said.

The NHS has been at the centre of a number of high-profile arguments over the interpretation of equality law and workplace regulations.

In January 2026, Darlington Memorial Hospital was found to have violated the dignity of a group of nurses who complained about a transgender colleague - a biological male who identified as a woman - being allowed to use the female changing rooms. The nurses were told they should change somewhere else if they objected.

The tribunal concluded that the trust had indirectly discriminated against them.

The nurses are currently seeking £400,000 from the NHS to cover their legal costs.

One of the nurses who brought the action, Bethany Hutchison, who is now president of the Darlington Nurses Union, says they welcome the "clear and necessary guidance" from NHSE, but the test will be whether trusts follow it.

"The Darlington nurses should never have had to take their own employer to court to secure privacy, dignity and lawful single-sex facilities," she said.

"Enforcement cannot continue to depend on the courage and personal sacrifice of individual nurses."

In Scotland, another employment tribunal found, in December 2025, that a nurse, Sandie Peggie, had been harassed by NHS Fife over its interpretation of rules on single sex spaces.

Peggie had complained about a doctor, who was a trans woman, using the female changing rooms.

She was suspended after raising concerns. The tribunal dismissed her other claims of discrimination and victimisation.

An appeal is under way and expected to reach the courts next year.

articles.title: The 1 Thing You Should Do If Your Period Pain Is Causing You to Miss Work
articles.summary: Dr. Annmarie Vilkins says severe period pain that causes you to miss work isn’t normal. You might be dealing with these undiagnosed conditions instead.
articles.body: TODAY’s Never Have I Ever series offers guidance about procedures and practices our trusted health experts would never participate in. Discover why they should be avoided and which healthy practices you should turn to instead. For some of us, it’s a twinge on the side, back pain and the telltale cramp in the pelvis. For others, period symptoms are debilitating, confining them to their beds. These aren’t the period symptoms you can push through, explains Dr. Annmarie Vilkins, obstetrician-gynecologist at Henry Ford Health. In fact, these aren’t the period symptoms you should ever have to push through. Severe menstrual pain, she says, the kind that impacts your quality of life, forcing you to stay home from work to cope, for example, is often the first sign you have a condition that deserves medical attention. Never Have I Ever: Thought Missing Work Because of My Period Was Normal “There is an expected amount of cramping that occurs with someone’s period,” Vilkins tells TODAY.com. “Period pain when somebody is down for the count because of their period, that’s not normal.” It is unfortunately common. Research, she says, has linked excruciating abdominal pain while you’re menstruating to missing work and reduced productivity. But the true cause might not even be your period at all. Instead, painful periods can be the result of conditions like endometriosis, adenomyosis and fibroids, which can be treated with surgery, medication and other procedures. Unfortunately, getting diagnosed with these conditions by a doctor who takes your pain seriously can be a challenge. A patient’s ultrasound, says Vilkins, might look totally normal. What the imaging can’t capture is how the hormone called prostaglandin, which causes the uterus to contract when you get your period, is making your uterus cramp especially aggressively because of these conditions, which can make it feel like there’s what Vilkins calls a “fireball in your pelvis.” As a result, some patients might go undiagnosed for decades, if not forever. What to Do Instead While it’s your healthcare provider’s responsibility to find and treat the source of your pain, Vilkins understands that many patients will ask for help and never get it. It’s critical, she says, to be “empowered and (be) a patient who’s going to be an advocate for their own health and say, ‘No, I’m coming to you because this really hurts, and I don’t think it’s normal.’” Vilkins recommends logging your pain. Rate it on a scale from 1-10, document the dates you feel pain and how long it lasts. Is it especially painful the week leading up to your period? Do you feel pain during intercourse? Take notes on how it affects your quality of life, and log everything you’ve already tried to ease the pain. If you suspect you have something specific, like endometriosis, say so. You might not be a doctor, but there are plenty of online resources that feature credible medical advice and can help you begin the process of identifying what you’re going through. From there, a doctor who takes you seriously will investigate. They’ll likely start with an ultrasound, which can spot fibroids. But, if your imaging looks normal, says Vilkins, you might need a blood test or a laparoscopy during which doctors make a small incision in your belly to locate any potential lesions that may indicate endometriosis or adenomyosis. In the end, you might not have any of these conditions and find that you have an overlapping condition that worsens when your period starts, such as constipation, says Vilkins. This will require you to involve other doctors. Whatever the reason for your pain, once you get your diagnosis, you can get the proper treatment, says Vilkins. That could be surgery or, in some cases, hormonal suppression with birth control or non-hormonal medications.

articles.title: Hillary Clinton concedes infamous 9/11 near-fainting episode in 2016 was a 'mistake' on her part
articles.summary: Hillary Clinton called campaigning with pneumonia during the 2016 race a "mistake" while discussing the viral 9/11 memorial ceremony video on a recent podcast.
articles.body: Former Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton revisited the video showing her appearing to stagger and nearly faint after a 9/11 commemoration ceremony in 2016, conceding on Wednesday that campaigning while having pneumonia was a "mistake." The former secretary of state spoke to Kara Swisher on their new joint podcast about Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico's nine-day absence from the campaign trail after he said he contracted the flu. His absence from public appearances led to a viral online rumor wrongly alleging that he had secretly been admitted to an Ohio mental health facility, which Clinton and Swisher said was "easily disproven." HILLARY CLINTON INCLUDES 2016 LOSS IN 'HARD TIMES' LIST FOR DEM VOTERS, INCLUDING 9/11, 2008 FINANCIAL CRISIS Clinton compared Talarico's experience to her own after the 2016 video went viral as she ran for president, arguing that critics portrayed her as being "on death's door." Swisher said that President Donald Trump was "quantumly sicker" than Clinton had been, though "they hide it," and asked Clinton to respond. "They tested me and they said, 'Oh, you've got pneumonia. You need to take like five or six days off.' I said, 'I can't do that.' And my doctor said, 'Well, that's what you should do.' And I thought, 'Well, yeah, that's what I should do.' But I'm campaigning and I have to show up on 9/11 because it means a lot to me since, as you know, I was a senator [during the attacks]. So, I kept going, which was a mistake," Clinton recalled. 'THE VIEW' CO-HOSTS CHALLENGE JOY BEHAR AFTER SHE SAYS TRUMP'S HEALTH GETS LESS MEDIA SCRUTINY THAN BIDEN'S She added, "They did have the video of me struggling to get to the car to be able to, you know, take some breaths and recover myself. From my perspective, it worked because it was just papering social media, papering traditional media. 'I was dying. I was lying about my health.' This is from a guy who has never given us an honest medical report ever. Ever." Fox News Digital reached out to Clinton's team for comment. White House spokesman Davis Ingle said Clinton should think about moving on from the 2016 election. "President Trump’s sharpness, unmatched energy, and historic accessibility stand in stark contrast to what we saw during the last administration, when Democrats and the legacy media intentionally covered up Joe Biden’s serious mental and physical decline from the American people," Ingle told Fox News Digital. "President Trump is working nonstop to solve problems and deliver on his promises, and he remains in excellent health. Meanwhile, Crooked Hillary Clinton is still whining about her spectacular 2016 election defeat. It’s time for Hillary to move on." According to a law enforcement source at the time, Clinton was described as "clearly having some type of medical episode" as she appeared to fall on her way to a van and required help from security. Clinton's campaign later released a statement confirming that she was fighting pneumonia and "felt overheated" at the time. articles.title: CDC sending a ‘disease detective’ to help stop measles outbreak in Pennsylvania
articles.summary: The CDC is sending one of its scientists to Pennsylvania to help curb the state’s growing measles outbreak, the agency said Thursday.
articles.body: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is sending one of its scientists to Pennsylvania to help curb the state’s growing measles outbreak, a CDC spokesperson said Thursday. That person, a “disease detective” within the agency’s Epidemic Intelligence Service, is scheduled to arrive later this week. It’s the CDC’s first in-person assistance to the state after a social media feud in August between Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. The two traded jabs following a press briefing where Shapiro announced that two unvaccinated people had died of measles complications and accused Kennedy of spreading vaccine misinformation. “I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said during the briefing. Kennedy then suggested that the deaths may have been “fabricated,” and that Shapiro was seeking to profit from them politically. Since August, six people diagnosed with measles have died in Pennsylvania, according to health officials and county coroners. The CDC has acknowledged two of the deaths on its measles outbreak website, saying the other measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania are “under review.” “CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health,” a CDC spokesperson wrote in an email Thursday, adding that director Dr. Erica Schwartz recommends the MMR vaccine “as the most effective way to prevent measles and protect against infection.” Pennsylvania is experiencing the nation’s worst measles outbreak in 30 years, with at least 1,222 confirmed cases and 225 hospitalizations, although doctors say the actual number of illnesses is likely much higher. The outbreak’s epicenter remains in Lancaster County, but is spreading across the state. The Pennsylvania Department of Health did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the CDC aid. The CDC team has previously sent teams to other states with large clusters of measles illnesses: Kansas, New Mexico, South Carolina, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin. Such deployments are usually short -term, about one to three weeks. They’re meant to help mobilize and streamline outbreak containment efforts. In addition to the deployment, the CDC is releasing nearly $4 million to aid the measles response efforts in Pennsylvania.

articles.title: 9 Simple Lifestyle Habits That Are Better for Improving Bone Density Than Taking Supplements
articles.summary: If you’re looking to improve your bone density and prevent fractures, try these science-backed lifestyle habits instead of relying on bone health supplements alone.
articles.body: Plenty of changes happen in our bodies as we get older, including the loss of bone density. It may be less obvious than sagging skin or wrinkles, but weak bones can seriously impact our quality of life and mobility. If you’re over a certain age, you’ve probably considered taking a bone health supplement. These consist mainly of two nutrients, calcium and vitamin D, which both help maintain bone density. Bone density refers to how strong the bones are, which is measured by the amount of minerals in a certain volume of bone tissue. The more densely packed, the stronger the bones — the more porous, the weaker. Low bone density (osteopenia) can lead to osteoporosis, which causes bones to become brittle and break easily. People who are at risk of having low bone density can benefit from taking bone health supplements, Dr. Jocelyn Wittstein, an orthopedic surgeon and co-author of “The Complete Bone and Joint Health Plan,” tells TODAY.com. These include people who can’t get enough calcium or vitamin D from their diet and post-menopausal women, for example. However, some research suggests that calcium and vitamin D supplements may not offer as meaningful protection against fractures for healthy adults who don’t have nutrient deficiencies or risk factors. Plus, bone health supplements can come with risks, especially when taken in high doses. For the average person, adopting a combination of lifestyle habits — including diet and exercise — is often safer and more effective than relying on bone health supplements, Wittstein notes. Habits to Try Instead of Taking Bone Health Supplements Whether you’re at risk of osteoporosis or not, you can still take everyday actions to help maintain bone density, prevent bone loss and protect against fractures. The average adult will reach peak bone mass around the age of 30, which is why most experts recommend to start building bone density in your 20s. However, it’s never too late to protect the bone density you have left. Here are nine science-backed bone health habits to try: Eat Foods High in Calcium and Vitamin D The key nutrients to prioritize in your diet for bone health are calcium and vitamin D. “I am very much in favor of getting these through food because it’s likely more effective and absorbs better,” says Wittstein. Calcium is an essential mineral that helps the body build and maintain strong bones. Vitamin D enables the body to absorb more calcium from food in the intestines, Wittstein explains. These two nutrients work together to boost bone health. If you increase your calcium intake without sufficient vitamin D levels, the body can only absorb 10-15% of that calcium — but if you get enough vitamin D, calcium absorption is closer to 40%, TODAY.com reported previously. Adults need 1,000 milligrams of calcium per day, but post-menopausal women need 1,200 milligrams. The recommended intake of vitamin D is 600 IUs for adults and 800 IUs for adults over the age of 70, says Wittstein. Foods high in calcium include milk, yogurt, cottage cheese, sardines and canned salmon (with the bones). If you’re plant-based, opt for tofu, soy milk and kale. Vitamin D is found in fatty fish such as trout and salmon, eggs and raw mushrooms, says Wittstein. In the U.S., milk and cereals are often fortified with vitamin D. And Foods Rich in Magnesium and Vitamin K2 It’s also important to eat whole foods rich in other nutrients that support bone health less directly — which you typically don’t get in a standalone supplement. These include magnesium, which helps convert vitamin D into its active form, and vitamin K2. “Vitamin K2 does seem to play a role in the mineralization of bone by activating something called osteocalcin, which basically helps direct the calcium to bone,” explains Wittstein. The average adult needs about 320-420 milligrams of magnesium per day. “There’s some plausible benefit of getting 100 micrograms a day of vitamin K2,” says Wittstein. Foods high in magnesium include pumpkin seeds, almonds, chia seeds, spinach and cashews. When it comes to vitamin K2, the best food source by far is natto, a fermented soybean product, says Wittstein. Other foods high in vitamin K2 include sauerkraut, kimchi, tempeh and kefir. Get Enough Protein Daily Muscle health goes hand in hand with bone health. That’s why it’s important to get enough protein every day to help build and repair muscle tissue. “You don’t need an excessive amount of protein for bone health,” says Wittstein. The average adult needs 1.2–1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day (or 0.54–0.73 grams per pound), according to the 2026-2030 Dietary Guidelines. If you weigh 150 pounds, that protein math works out to 81–109 grams per day, and about 20–40 grams of protein per meal. Instead of relying on protein shakes or bars, which are often highly processed, try to get your protein from whole food sources like lean meat, seafood, legumes, eggs, and dairy. Prioritize Fiber “One of the major components that contributes to bone health is getting adequate dietary fiber,” says Wittstein. It does so through what’s called the “gut-bone axis.” Fiber isn’t digested by the body. Instead, it travels to the gut, where it feeds healthy bacteria. The microbes ferment the fiber, producing short-chain fatty acids. “These have an anti-inflammatory effect by basically inhibiting some of the processes that lead to bone breakdown, and inhibiting cartilage breakdown,” Wittstein adds. Most American fall short of the recommended daily fiber intake — which is 25 grams per day for women and 38 for men. If you’re looking to increase your intake, eat more fiber-rich foods, including beans and legumes, raspberries, broccoli, pears, squash, oats or quinoa. Wittstein also recommends getting healthy fats and avoiding foods that can worsen inflammation. Take Up Resistance Training One of the most important habits to support bone health is regular resistance training. “Resistance training two or three days a week will improve bone density,” says Wittstein. Some of the best strength training exercises for bone density are compound movements that “also involve carrying weight in a way that’s loading your spine and hips,” says Wittstein. (Compound movements are exercises that work multiple muscles groups at a time.) Examples include weighted squats, overhead presses, deadlifts and the farmer’s carry. “Any exercise that’s weight-bearing is going to have some benefit. ... and (doing) more load-bearing exercises does slow the loss of bone density,” Wittstein adds. Lower-impact resistance exercises include push-ups, planks, lunges and moves using resistance bands. Incorporate Impact into Your Routine “If your body allows and you don’t have restrictions, participate in some kind of impact training,” Wittstein says. Impact training subjects the body to mechanical force, which occurs when we land on the ground or strike an object, TODAY.com reported previously. Think jumping or stomping. The force of the impact sends vibrations through the cells of the bones, which leads to more bone formation, Wittstein explains. Impact training is especially helpful for the hip region, which is prone to weakening and fractures as we age. The best impact training exercise for you will depend on your health and injury risk. Too much impact can do harm. The easiest impact training exercise is brisk walking. From there, you can graduate to heel drops, stomping, jogging, running and squat jumps. Always consult with your doctor before trying impact training, especially if you’re older or at risk of osteoporosis. Work on Balance and Mobility Balance and mobility exercises can protect bone health by preventing falls and therefore fractures. Falls are the leading cause of injury among adults ages 65 and older, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In order to assess your balance and mobility level, you can try two simple tests (no equipment needed): the sit-to-stand test and the “Y balance test.” Try to incorporate exercises for mobility and balance into your weekly exercise routine, says Wittstein. These include: single-leg lifts, sideways walking, tai chi and yoga. “It’s also good to incorporate agility work, or exercises where you’re having to move your feet quickly. These are the skills that will ultimately keep you from tripping and falling,” says Wittstein. Avoid Excessive Alcohol or Nicotine Along with a healthy diet, limiting alcohol may help support bone health. “Drinking more than two alcoholic beverages per day has been shown to increase fracture risk,” says Wittstein. “You definitely want to avoid nicotine of all forms,” says Wittstein. This includes cigarettes, vaping and even nicotine patches. “Any systemic form of nicotine is a risk for bone loss.” Get Screened “One problem is people just don’t go to the doctor, or don’t have a primary care doctor,” says Wittstein. It’s important to get an idea of your underlying health, nutrient levels and risk factors. “I think it’s reasonable to make sure you’re not vitamin D deficient,” Wittstein adds. Healthcare providers can also screen you for low bone density using a DXA scan, an x-ray that measures the mineral content of bones, per the Cleveland Clinic. Regular DXA screenings are recommended for women ages 65 and older and men ages 70 and older, and younger people who have risk factors for osteoporosis. Always talk to your doctor if you have any questions.

articles.title: Weight-loss drugs may fight 7 serious health problems before the pounds even come off
articles.summary: GLP-1 medications like semaglutide and tirzepatide may be repairing joints, calming inflammation, and protecting vital organs before any weight loss occurs.
articles.body: GLP-1 medications may provide health benefits that extend beyond weight loss, according to a growing body of research. From reducing cardiovascular risks to potentially easing joint pain and inflammation, studies suggest these drugs may affect multiple systems throughout the body. Here are seven potential benefits beyond shedding pounds. POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS STRATEGY SHOWS SURPRISING POTENTIAL FOR CHRONIC PAIN RELIEF No. 1: Protecting heart health Research suggests semaglutide — the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy — may provide cardiovascular benefits beyond those associated with weight loss. A major study published in The Lancet found that semaglutide reduced the risk of heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular death among people with existing cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity. The benefits were observed across different body weights and were not fully explained by weight loss. No. 2: Reducing joint pain and improving mobility GLP-1 medications have been linked to reduced joint pain, although researchers are still investigating how much of the benefit comes from weight loss versus other effects. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The STEP 9 clinical trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, found that semaglutide significantly reduced knee osteoarthritis pain and improved physical function among adults with obesity. No. 3: Promoting kidney health GLP-1 medications may help protect kidney function through several mechanisms, including improvements in blood sugar, blood pressure and inflammation. GLP-1 BOOM COULD RESHAPE RESTAURANT BARS AS DINERS CUT BACK ON ALCOHOL In the landmark FLOW trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, semaglutide reduced the risk of major kidney-related complications and cardiovascular death by 24% among patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease. No. 4: Reducing liver inflammation and scarring MASH, or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, is a more severe form of fatty liver disease involving inflammation and liver cell damage. Research suggests GLP-1 medications may help improve liver health, although the extent to which these benefits occur independently of weight loss remains under investigation. A clinical trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine found that semaglutide improved liver tissue findings among patients with MASH, including reductions in inflammation and liver scarring. Researchers found that 62.9% of semaglutide recipients experienced resolution of MASH without worsening liver fibrosis, compared with 34.3% receiving placebo. No. 5: Reducing respiratory flare-ups Real-world research presented at the European Respiratory Society Congress has linked GLP-1 medications to fewer asthma attacks and COPD flare-ups. Researchers believe the drugs' potential anti-inflammatory effects may play a role, although additional studies are needed to determine whether the medications directly improve respiratory health. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES No. 6: Supporting mental health and curbing addiction The brain contains GLP-1 receptors in regions involved in regulating appetite, emotions, motivation and responses to rewards. Emerging research suggests semaglutide may have potential benefits for mental health and addiction. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP An observational study published on the preprint server medRxiv linked semaglutide use to lower rates of substance-related and mood disorders. However, the findings have not been peer-reviewed and do not establish that the medication caused the reductions. No. 7: Soothing severe skin conditions GLP-1-based medications are also being investigated for their potential benefits in inflammatory skin conditions, including psoriasis. A clinical trial published in JAMA Dermatology found that adding tirzepatide to an existing psoriasis treatment improved skin clearance among adults with moderate to severe psoriasis and overweight or obesity. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Researchers are continuing to investigate whether these benefits result from weight loss, reduced inflammation or a combination of factors. The effects of GLP-1 medications can vary by drug and individual, and patients should consult a healthcare provider about potential risks and benefits.

articles.title: A mother’s touch helps premature babies grow strong in Gaza
articles.summary: At Nasser Hospital, a kangaroo mother care pilot programme helps vulnerable newborns.
articles.body:
Khan Younis, Gaza Strip – For 11 days after giving birth last month, Rania Fadel could not hold her newborn son.

The 24-year-old gave birth to twin boys, Ilyas and Yahya, on September 25.

While Yahya was born healthy, Ilyas was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, where he remained for nearly two weeks.

Born prematurely, Ilyas weighed just 1.4 kilogrammes (3 pounds) at birth, according to his mother. He had medical issues affecting his blood and lungs, she said, and needed specialised care in an incubator.

Rania herself was recovering from a Caesarean section when her son was taken into intensive care. For days, she could not hold him.

“When they called me to hold him, I rushed over,” she recalled. “I was in a hurry to get to him. It was such a feeling.”

As Ilyas’s condition improved and he moved from intensive care to the hospital’s neonatal care unit, Rania was able to hold him against her bare chest, introducing her to a form of care for low-birthweight newborns known as kangaroo mother care, part of a newly-launched programme at the hospital.

It involves prolonged skin-to-skin contact between a caregiver – ideally the mother – and baby, with exclusive breast milk feeding, and has been shown to have important health benefits for premature and low-birthweight babies.

“I was so happy. It was such a beautiful feeling,” Rania said.

During the session, a nurse helped Rania position Ilyas against her chest, with his skin touching hers. Rania said he remained there for about 90 minutes.

“He started breastfeeding from me, and he stayed a little longer,” she said. “I felt he was improving.”

For Rania, the contact also brought a sense of closeness after days of separation.

“The baby feels that his mother is there,” she said. “He feels safe. Honestly, it makes me very happy.”

Kangaroo mother care involves placing a baby against a parent’s bare chest for skin-to-skin contact, alongside breastfeeding and appropriate medical care.

For premature and low-birthweight babies, it can help regulate body temperature, support breastfeeding and improve health outcomes.

World Health Organization (WHO) guidance says that kangaroo mother care has been shown to reduce neonatal mortality by 32 percent, and mortality by six months of age by 25 percent, compared with conventional care.

At Nasser Medical Complex, Khawla al-Madhoun, director of nursing at the hospital’s maternity and neonatal departments, described it as an integrated approach to newborn care that supports growth and strengthens the bond between mother and baby.

“When we place a baby on the mother’s chest, it helps the baby grow,” she said.

“We have seen babies who were unwell or underweight begin to grow faster with kangaroo care. This can help them leave the hospital sooner.”

The hospital has begun introducing kangaroo care through a pilot programme supported by WHO, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), and the UN Population Fund (UNFPA). The agencies announced the initiative at Nasser Hospital in September, but the practice is being introduced gradually in its external neonatal care unit, where babies stay with their mothers, and in maternity wards after delivery.

Al-Madhoun said the team was also preparing a dedicated room and seeking equipment to make the sessions more comfortable.

The team aims for longer periods of skin-to-skin contact – WHO recommends at least eight hours per day – although its immediate target is at least two hours, depending on each family’s circumstances.

At Nasser, the team is currently prioritising babies who are medically stable and do not require oxygen support. Nurses monitor their vital signs and assess them throughout the process.

Al-Madhoun stressed that the technique cannot replace an incubator or other treatment when a baby needs intensive care.

“It can help babies grow, gain weight and leave the hospital earlier, but some babies need other interventions, such as respiratory support,” she said. “Those babies still need the incubator and the care it provides.”

The need for specialised newborn care comes as Gaza’s health system continues to struggle with damaged facilities, shortages of equipment and overcrowded neonatal units.

Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, Gaza had eight neonatal intensive care units with a total of 178 incubators, according to UNICEF.

By November 2024, three of those units had been destroyed by Israel, and the number of available incubators had fallen to about 54, a reduction of 70 percent. The shortage of equipment, compounded by limited supplies of fuel and electricity as a result of Israeli restrictions, put premature newborns at serious risk.

Israeli strikes have continued since an October 2025 “ceasefire”. Despite this supposed truce, and despite the delivery of some new equipment, the shortage of incubators and other equipment has persisted.

In May, UNICEF said it and its partners had supplied incubators and ventilators to hospitals in Gaza, while warning that neonatal units were still managing large numbers of fragile infants with limited equipment, space and power.

The war in Gaza has worsened living conditions for pregnant women with economic hardship, food shortages, poor nutrition and the harsh realities of displacement, including cooking over open fires and carrying water.

“These conditions have contributed to the rise in premature births and babies born with low birth weight who need specialised neonatal care,” al-Madhoun said.

Meanwhile, repeated displacement and overcrowding have placed further pressure on hospitals, including Nasser Medical Complex, which is already struggling with limited space and shortages of incubators and other essential neonatal equipment.

Linda Abu Nasira’s baby girl is only three days old.

The infant initially developed a fever, which has since subsided, according to 23-year-old Linda.

As her daughter was being treated and breastfed, Linda was learning how to hold her against her chest under the guidance of the medical team.

The sessions were brief. Linda said she held her daughter against her chest for about 30 minutes at a time, repeating the process roughly every two hours, according to the instructions she had received.

“She is a little better than yesterday,” Linda said. “Little by little.”

Away from the hospital, Linda lives in a tent in al-Mawasi, in Khan Younis, where she is raising her two older children – aged three and two – while caring for her newborn.

She described the conditions as difficult, particularly when it comes to securing food and drinking water.

“We try to manage,” she said. “But it is not like before, or like the conditions you would expect when giving birth.”

She does not know how long the baby will need to remain under observation in the hospital’s external neonatal care unit.

“As a mother, it means a lot to me to feel that I am helping my daughter recover,” Linda said. “I hope she will recover and be discharged as soon as possible.”
